objectives: Secure a negotiated settlement with the UK that avoids retaliatory withdrawal of concessions and avoids a joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA disapplication dispute
Preserve the EU's ability to implement a permanent TRQ/tariff regime on the 41 lines to address non-market-economy overcapacity, without derailing the Council's June timetable

Obtain UK agreement (or at least acquiescence) to a country-specific or otherwise workable UK share of the TRQ that is defensible as 'substantially equivalent' compensation, minimising the credibility gap between EU claims of compensation and actual UK trade loss
Avoid setting a precedent in this settlement that unduly constrains the EU's parallel handling of Turkey, Korea, India and Japan's claims
Keep the disapplication of FTA tariff reductions for non-EEA partners intact if possible, but be willing to trade UK-specific carve-outs or transitional treatment if that secures settlement
Protect EU exporters' existing quota allocations under the UK's own steel safeguard from being unwound or reduced in retaliation
Maintain the EU's institutional credibility and working relationship with the UK Geneva team for future goods files, regardless of outcome on this file
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement within the four rounds that the UK capital accepts, involving a TRQ/compensation package the UK can present domestically as adequate, EU exporters' UK safeguard quotas preserved or improved, no UK retaliatory withdrawal, and no UK alignment with Japan/Korea on FTA disapplication retaliation. The EU's 50% out-of-quota rate and permanent legal footing for the regime survive intact or nearly so. Failure: no settlement, UK withdraws substantially equivalent concessions after six months, UK joins Japan/Korea in a coordinated FTA response, and/or Brussels has to explain to Council/member states why a politically sensitive steel measure triggered a wider trade dispute with a close partner just as domestic legislation is being finalised.
declaration.approach: Open by restating the EU's legal position (non-market-economy overcapacity, need for permanent footing) but signal early that volume, allocation method, administration, duration/review clause, and FTA treatment are all genuinely open for this negotiation — since Brussels has left these undetermined, I have real room to construct a package. Prioritise concessions that are cheap for the EU but valuable to the UK: a UK-specific country share (rather than pure global first-come-first-served, which structurally disadvantages a geographically concentrated, single-market-dependent exporter like the UK), a review clause, and a phased or higher initial volume. Use the FTA-disapplication provision as a bargaining chip — the UK cares about this both directly and because it fears alignment with Japan/Korea; offering to soften or delay it for the UK specifically could be inexpensive for the EU while being highly valuable to the UK, and it also serves the EU's separate interest of preventing a UK-Japan-Korea coalition from forming. Avoid discussing Turkey/Korea/India/Japan specifics to keep those claims separate. Use Phase 2 consultations to test Brussels' flexibility on volume/share and to flag the coalition risk as a reason to move. Sequence concessions across rounds rather than front-loading, to see the UK's real floor before committing, but do not let the process drag to Round 4 without a credible offer on the table, since a no-deal outcome carries real escalation risk I've been told to avoid.

parties.who: UK (DBT / UK Mission Geneva)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A country-specific UK share of the TRQ (not exposed to global first-come-first-served competition with Turkey/Korea), a volume that materially reduces the cut to their 2.4mt baseline, retention of FTA-equivalent tariff treatment under the TCA or an explicit carve-out from the disapplication provision, a review clause, and protection/continuation of EU exporters' quota under the UK's own safeguard as a mutual de-escalation move. They will also want to preserve leverage via the Japan/Korea coalition threat and their own parallel Article XXVIII process, and need a deal defensible to a steel-producing constituency with concentrated regional employment.

parties.who: Brussels (Commission mandate-holders, Council/TPC, member states)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A permanent legal footing for the steel regime that visibly targets non-market-economy overcapacity, minimal erosion of the 50%/400kt headline numbers, protection of steel-producing member states' interests, but also sensitivity from steel-consuming member states to not choke off supply entirely; strong preference to conclude by June and avoid a WTO dispute or retaliation that complicates the EU's broader trade agenda.

parties.who: Japan and Korea (via reserved rights / informal pressure on UK)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To use the FTA-disapplication issue as a lever to build a coalition with the UK against the EU's measure, protecting their own FTA-based access and setting a precedent against selective disapplication; they want to avoid being isolated as 'non-market-economy adjacent' targets and would benefit from the UK amplifying the systemic objection.

parties.who: Turkey and India (reserved rights, larger/other volumes)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Their own bilateral compensation or carve-outs proportional to their trade shares; they are watching the UK settlement as a possible benchmark but are being handled on a separate track, so they want consistency without necessarily wanting to coordinate with the UK.

objectives: Secure UK agreement to the modification within the four rounds so the Council can vote in June

Preserve a TRQ regime that meaningfully restricts volume and is administered in a way that lets the EU manage country-level exposure (i.e. avoid a purely global first-come-first-served pool that non-market-economy exporters could exploit fastest)

Obtain a UK-specific quota share that is calibrated below recent trade volumes but large enough, combined with other terms, to constitute credible 'substantially equivalent' compensation and avoid UK retaliation
Retain the ability to disapply FTA-origin cumulation/preference erosion risk from third countries, while being pragmatic about UK treatment specifically to get a deal
Avoid setting a precedent in this settlement that other principal suppliers (Turkey, Korea) can point to as a floor for their own claims
Keep member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors and steel-producing sectors both broadly satisfied with the outcome reported to the Trade Policy Committee
Secure some reciprocal comfort on treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own steel safeguard, ideally without conceding EU flexibility on the core TRQ design
Preserve room for a review clause that lets the EU tighten further if overcapacity pressure continues, rather than locking in generous terms indefinitely
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a settlement inside four rounds that keeps the TRQ regime intact in substance (meaningful out-of-quota rate, a volume and allocation method the Commission controls rather than one dictated by the UK, no broad carve-outs that gut the measure) while giving the UK enough — a country-specific or ring-fenced share, phased implementation, or a review clause — that they accept without retaliating and without this becoming the template Turkey and Korea demand. Failure is either (a) no deal, forcing the fallback 50%/400,000t global FCFS regime with no review clause, missing the June Council vote, and inviting UK retaliation that hits EU exporters into the UK plus reputational cost with member states who wanted a negotiated outcome; or (b) a deal so generous to the UK that it invites parallel demands from Turkey/Korea/India/Japan, undermines the volume-reduction objective that is my actual policy purpose, and draws criticism from steel-producing member states.
declaration.approach: Open firm — restate the proposal as the baseline and frame the 50%/400k/global-FCFS as the status quo the UK should want to improve on, not a starting point I intend to move far from. Use the multi-round structure to concede slowly: first on administration/process items (licensing method, review clause, phasing) which are lower cost to me, before moving on volume or country-specific share, which is the UK's real ask. Signal flexibility on a review clause and on transitional arrangements as a way to buy a lower headline volume commitment. Try to keep the FTA-disapplication text as leverage — something I can trade away specifically for UK concessions on the TCA/circumvention provisions or on treatment of EU exporters in the UK's own safeguard. Watch for signs the UK capital is willing to accept less than full historical volumes if given predictability (duration, review clause, licensing certainty) rather than pure tonnage. Keep Geneva-table language generic/defensible since it's visible to the UK seat, and reserve real trade-offs for the private capital consultation. Do not reveal that I lack a hard settlement figure — anchor expectations around defensibility to the Trade Policy Committee and steel producers.

parties.who: UK Geneva seat / UK Mission
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To maximise the UK-specific quota share and minimise the out-of-quota rate impact, secure a review clause or sunset, avoid the FTA-disapplication provision being used against UK-origin steel, and get some reciprocal comfort on EU treatment under the UK's own safeguard — while under real pressure not to let this collapse given the damage a no-deal fallback does to UK producers.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade / Ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Political cover to show they protected UK steel jobs and secured 'fair' access; likely willing to accept a defined country-specific allocation and phased/reviewed terms rather than insist on full historical volume, but will resist being seen to fold, and will weigh the parallel leverage of the UK's own Article XXVIII/safeguard process against EU exporters.

parties.who: European Commissioner / Council mandate holders
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A concluded deal in time for the June Council vote that visibly reduces steel import volumes and is defensible as 'substantially equivalent' compensation, without triggering retaliation elsewhere (especially given US tariff threats) or creating precedent problems with Turkey/Korea/India/Japan.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (e.g. Germany, France, Italy, Spain)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum restriction on imports, strong out-of-quota rate, minimal carve-outs, and scepticism toward generous UK-specific treatment.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Sufficient tariff-free volume and administrative simplicity (avoiding punitive out-of-quota costs) to protect input costs for their industries; some sympathy for a negotiated, less disruptive outcome with the UK.

parties.who: Turkey, Korea, India, Japan (parallel claimants)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To watch this settlement closely as a benchmark for their own claims; Turkey and Korea especially will expect treatment at least as favourable given their larger volumes, so I should avoid over-conceding to the UK in ways that raise the cost of those parallel settlements.

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK share of the TRQ (not global first-come-first-served) sized to reflect recent trade volumes, so UK exporters have predictable, defensible access rather than racing EU/global competitors for a shared pool.

Push out-of-quota tariff and in-quota volume toward something UK steelmakers can live with — ideally a much larger duty-free tonnage than 400,000t globally implies for the UK, or a UK-specific quota close to historical UK export volumes (~2.4mt) with growth/review mechanism.

Prevent or narrow the disapplication of FTA-equivalent treatment as applied to the UK specifically — press for the UK to be treated at least as well as other principal supplying interests, ideally preserving TCA-linked treatment given the depth of UK-EU trade integration.
Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration rather than a permanent, unreviewable settlure, to allow revisiting if EU import patterns or non-market-economy overcapacity dynamics change.
Extract clarity on compensation elsewhere in EU schedule as a fallback/parallel lever, in case volume/allocation concessions stall.
Protect UK's own steel safeguard flexibility — avoid being locked into reciprocal concessions on EU exporters' UK quota shares that we are not ready to give.

Avoid escalation into joint FTA retaliation with Japan/Korea unless the EU proves completely inflexible — keep that as a credible but unused threat, since UK's own steel measure and TCA relationship with the EU are separate long-term files I must keep workable.
Preserve working relationship with EU counterpart across other Geneva goods files regardless of outcome here.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a settlement that gives UK exporters a country-specific or otherwise ring-fenced share of the TRQ materially above what a global first-come-first-served pool would deliver, with a workable out-of-quota rate, a review clause, and no unilateral UK concession on EU access to the UK's own safeguard quotas beyond what London has authorised. Success also means not being forced into premature concessions in early rounds. Failure is arriving at Round 4 with no more than the EU's opening offer (50% bound rate, 400,000t global FCFS, FTA disapplication intact, no review), forcing London into a no-deal path with retaliatory withdrawal and lasting damage to UK-EU trade relations, or alternatively caving early to EU terms that London views as inadequate given no settlement figure was authorised.
declaration.approach: Hold a firm, patient posture in early rounds: state clearly that the opening EU offer is unacceptable and would be materially damaging to UK industry, without immediately naming a target number, to avoid anchoring low. Use Phase 1 to probe the EU's real red lines (is 400,000t/50%/global-FCFS/FTA-disapplication all equally fixed, or are some elements more negotiable than others given the Council timeline?). Use Phase 2 consultations honestly with London to relay EU flexibility (or lack of it) and seek an actual settlement range/mandate rather than negotiating blind. Exploit the EU's June deadline as leverage — they need closure faster than we do reputationally, though we too face industry pressure. Keep the Japan/Korea joint retaliation option visible but do not commit to it; use it rhetorically as a sign that EU actions are generating broader systemic friction, which increases pressure on the EU to be reasonable with us specifically to avoid multiplying fronts. Do not concede on UK's own safeguard treatment of EU exporters early — keep that as a card to trade late for a better UK-specific TRQ share or carve-out. Aim to convert the negotiation from 'global pool' framing to 'country-specific share' framing as the single most important structural win, since that shapes everything else downstream.

parties.who: EU Commission (Geneva negotiator)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Conclude quickly enough to hit the June Council vote; lock in the 50%/400,000t/global FCFS/FTA-disapplication package with minimal changes; offer only modest, cheap compensation (e.g. on unrelated schedule lines) rather than restructuring the TRQ; will resist country-specific shares because that invites similar demands from Turkey, Korea, Japan, India and complicates their internal member-state politics (steel producers vs manufacturers).

parties.who: UK capital (DBT/Ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Protect UK steel jobs and production sites concentrated in a few constituencies; avoid being seen as weak against a measure seen as protectionist overreach; will want tangible volume/share wins before accepting anything, but also wary of a no-deal outcome that triggers six-month withdrawal uncertainty and further UK industry harm; likely cautious about linking this to UK's own safeguard concessions to the EU.

parties.who: Turkey and Korea
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Their own larger-volume principal supplying interest deals with the EU, handled separately; they may shape the precedent for country-specific shares which could help or hinder UK's ask depending on how EU treats them.

parties.who: Japan and Korea (re: joint FTA retaliation approach)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To recruit UK into a joint dispute/retaliation against EU's FTA disapplication text, adding pressure on the EU; useful leverage but risks entangling UK in a broader systemic fight and complicating our bilateral settlement and TCA relationship — treat as an instrument, not a commitment.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (via Council/TPC)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum protection, minimal TRQ volume, resistant to UK-specific carve-outs that dilute protection.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Larger TRQ, cheaper input steel, may quietly support more generous UK access if it eases input costs — potential internal EU leverage point to probe.

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK share of the TRQ (not global first-come-first-served) sized to approximately protect recent trade flows (~2.4mt), with headroom for growth
Push out-of-quota rate down or negotiate a phased/lower rate for UK-origin steel above quota, or at minimum a credible glide path
Prevent disapplication of TCA-equivalent tariff treatment for UK steel — treat UK as at least equivalent to FTA partners, ideally carved closer to EEA treatment given TCA depth
Obtain a review clause with a defined trigger and timeline so the regime isn't a permanent one-way ratchet
Secure product-line carve-outs or higher sub-quotas for the narrower range of products where UK exports are concentrated
Obtain compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule if volume/price terms cannot be fully protected, to offset economic harm and give ministers a defensible package
Protect negotiating room on the UK's own safeguard vis-à-vis EU exporters as a bargaining chip, not a giveaway
Avoid a breakdown that forces reliance solely on retaliatory withdrawal, which is slow (6 months), imperfect in value-matching, and doesn't fix the underlying market access problem for UK producers
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a UK-specific quota share close to or above recent trade volumes, a materially lower or phased out-of-quota rate than 50%, continued FTA-equivalent (TCA-linked) treatment preserved or a bespoke UK carve-out, a review clause within 2-3 years, and/or compensation package sufficient that ministers and industry judge the plants' continued investment case intact. Failure: UK dumped into the global FCFS pool alongside Turkey/Korea (who will exhaust it fast given larger volumes), UK steel treated worse than other FTA partners despite TCA depth, no review mechanism, no compensation, and no credible narrative for ministers to sell to industry — leaving retaliation as the only recourse, which is slow and doesn't restore market access.
declaration.approach: Anchor early on the core ask: a UK-specific quota share reflecting historical trade share, explicitly linked to the TCA to resist the FTA-disapplication clause, since being lumped in with Turkey/Korea in a global FCFS pool would be worst-case (they have larger volumes and would exhaust it fast). Use the UK's own steel safeguard and its EU-specific country allocations as the primary lever — offer improved EU access there only against real EU concessions (quota share, rate, review clause), not as a unilateral goodwill gesture. Keep the subsidy option in reserve; don't signal it, since revealing it weakens our leverage by suggesting we can absorb a bad deal. Escalate gradually across rounds: open ambitious (country-specific share, near-zero out-of-quota rate for in-scope volumes, TCA carve-out, review clause), identify EU's real red lines (Council politics, protection of domestic producers) in consultation phases, and trade down deliberately — sacrificing rate ambition for volume certainty or vice versa, and using compensation-elsewhere as a fallback if TRQ terms can't move far enough. Coordinate closely with capital between rounds to make sure Geneva doesn't over-commit ahead of ministerial tolerance, and preserve the option of walking away to retaliation/subsidy route if the deal doesn't clear the bar ministers care about (industry survival).

parties.who: European Commission (Geneva/DG Trade)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To conclude a legally durable TRQ regime by June in time for Council vote, protect EU domestic steel producers from non-market-economy overcapacity, minimise compensation elsewhere in its schedule, and manage competing member state interests (steel producers wanting protection vs manufacturers wanting cheap inputs). Likely resistant to generous UK-specific carve-outs since Turkey/Korea claims are parallel and any UK deal sets a precedent.

parties.who: UK steel industry (producers, 2 plants at risk)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum preserved tariff-free access to the EU market, certainty/duration in any quota allocation, and a signal robust enough to justify further investment rather than closure. Will judge outcome partly on volume secured, partly on rate, partly on political optics.

parties.who: UK downstream manufacturers / steel-consuming sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Continued access to affordable EU steel inputs if UK's own safeguard measure terms are adjusted; will resist UK giving away too much access to EU exporters under the UK safeguard without gaining enough in return.

parties.who: Turkey and Korea (parallel Art. XXVIII claimants)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Their own large country shares or high global quota volumes; their bulk will crowd out UK access if the TRQ remains global FCFS, making UK's case for country-specific allocation stronger by contrast.

parties.who: UK Ministers / DBT leadership
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically defensible deal that visibly protects steel jobs and the two at-risk plants, without having to immediately commit to costly subsidisation; want to be seen as tough negotiators securing 'best available terms'.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (e.g. France, Germany, Italy, Spain)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Strong protection, high out-of-quota rates, tight quotas — pushing the Commission toward a harder line domestically, limiting Commission's room to offer the UK generous terms.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Continued access to cheap imported steel (including UK-origin), potentially a moderating influence pushing the Commission toward a larger or more liberal TRQ than pure producer interests would prefer.

public_message: The European Union opens this Article XXVIII consultation on the basis of the measure as notified: a bound rate of 50% ad valorem on the 41 lines in question, with a global tariff rate quota of 400,000 tonnes per year administered first-come first-served, and disapplication of FTA-derived reductions for UK-origin steel outside the EEA. We recognise the UK's principal supplying interest and are ready to discuss compensation within the scope of this process — including the allocation method, administration, duration, review mechanisms, and treatment of specific product lines where UK exports are concentrated. We are not opening with a fixed settlement figure. We want to understand the UK's priorities before we move numbers, and we would rather find a negotiated outcome here than see this spill into retaliatory action or parallel disputes with other claimants.

other_terms: FTA-derived tariff reductions on UK-origin steel disapplied for all FTA partners other than EEA members
Open to discussing a country-specific UK tranche, review clause, and product-line carve-outs as the negotiation proceeds

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A counter-proposal focused on a UK-specific tranche within the pool, a review clause, and objections to the FTA disapplication provision as it affects the TCA and circumvention risk
expectations.why: The UK's volumes are large relative to the notified pool and concentrated in a narrow product range, so their leverage will focus on tranche size and product carve-outs rather than the headline bound rate

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Confirmation of how far Geneva may move on allocation and duration before the next round
expectations.why: Need negotiating room on the softer variables (allocation, review clause, carve-outs) to keep the UK at the table without pre-committing on volume or rate in round one

private_rationale: Anchoring on the notified text in round one preserves EU leverage and keeps Brussels' mandate intact, while the offer to discuss allocation, tranche, review clause and carve-outs signals genuine engagement — important both to keep this WTO-consistent and to reduce the risk of the UK aligning with Japan and Korea on FTA retaliation. Conceding numbers now would be premature and would weaken our position before we know the UK's real priorities; better to draw those out in phase 2/3 of later rounds.

public_message: The UK notes that the measure as notified represents a reduction of tariff-free access on the order of 85% against our recent trading history, before any consideration of how a global first-come first-served pool would actually be exhausted in practice. Given that Turkey and Korea ship larger volumes into the same pool, a global FCFS quota would foreseeably see UK exporters priced out of tariff-free access within weeks of the quota year opening, regardless of the headline 400,000 tonnes. That is not a basis for negotiation consistent with our principal supplying interest under Article XXVIII. Our starting position is a country-specific allocation reflecting recent representative trade — in the region of our historical average of 2.4 million tonnes — administered through a licensing mechanism that gives UK exporters predictable access rather than a race to the docks. We also do not accept the disapplication of FTA-derived treatment for UK-origin steel as a matter of principle: the UK is not a non-market-economy overcapacity source, and singling out UK-origin product for removal of preferences the TCA established, while EEA states retain theirs, sits awkwardly alongside the EU's stated rationale for this measure. We are open to discussing product-line carve-outs where UK exports are concentrated, duration, and a review clause, but we are not going to treat the notified measure as the baseline from which we negotiate downward. We would rather resolve this here than see it escalate, but firmness now is in both our interests if we want a durable outcome.

other_terms: UK-specific licensed tranche set at recent historical trade average (2.4mt/year), not subject to global FCFS competition
No disapplication of TCA tariff preferences for UK-origin steel
Carve-outs for product lines where UK export concentration is highest, to be identified by line
Review clause at end of year 2 to reassess volumes and rate based on actual trade flows
Reciprocal commitment to review treatment of EU exporters under UK's own steel safeguard in parallel, without linking the two legally

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A substantive counter on volume and allocation method, and a response on whether FTA disapplication is truly non-negotiable or a bargaining chip
expectations.why: The EU opened without a number and asked for our priorities; we've given a clear anchor. Their response will reveal whether Council mandate has real flexibility or whether 400k/global/FCFS is closer to their true floor.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Confirmation of whether 2.4mt is the right anchor figure or whether we should be prepared to move off it, and steer on how hard to hold the FTA/TCA point
expectations.why: I have not been given a settlement figure and need capital's view on the acceptable floor before round 2, particularly on the country-specific tranche size and the TCA disapplication issue which has legal as well as commercial dimensions

private_rationale: Opening high and anchored on historical trade volume is standard practice and consistent with instructions to be firm — conceding early invites further erosion. The country-specific/licensing demand directly attacks the mechanism (global FCFS) that would functionally gut UK access even if the headline pool looks reasonable, and forces the EU to negotiate on allocation method rather than just volume. Raising the TCA/FTA disapplication point hard and early is important because it's a distinct legal grievance beyond the TRQ volume math, and the EU including EEA exemption while excluding the UK specifically is a discrimination point worth pressing given the EU's own stated 'non-market economy' rationale. I'm holding off on committing to the Japan/Korea joint dispute route — flagging it implicitly ('escalate') without committing keeps pressure on the EU without prematurely coordinating with other claimants, which London hasn't authorised and which could complicate our own separate Art XXVIII leverage over EU-origin imports into the UK.

report: Round 1 opened with us restating the notified measure in full (50% bound rate, 400,000t global FCFS TRQ, FTA disapplication for UK-origin steel) and signalling openness on allocation, administration, duration, review and product lines, without moving off the notified baseline. UK's opening position was firm and well-argued: they reject the notified measure as a starting baseline, characterise it as an ~85% cut to their tariff-free access once Turkey/Korea's larger volumes are factored into a global FCFS pool, and opened by demanding a country-specific allocation close to their full historical average (2.4Mt) administered via licensing rather than FCFS. They also explicitly rejected the FTA disapplication as inconsistent with our stated non-market-economy rationale, noting the asymmetry with EEA treatment. They did signal flexibility on product-line carve-outs, duration and a review clause, and closed by saying they'd rather resolve this in Geneva than escalate — which I read as a genuine preference for settlement, not just posturing. No mention yet of the Turkey/Korea/Japan coalition angle, but the FTA disapplication objection is exactly the wedge that could pull the UK toward joining them in a parallel dispute if we don't address it.

recommendation.reasoning: The gap between 400,000t global FCFS and a 2.4Mt country-specific demand is wide, but the UK's opening is a bargaining position, not their floor — the flexibility they signalled on carve-outs, duration and review gives us room. I recommend we test a country-specific UK tranche carved out of a modestly expanded global pool (not the full historical average), retain the 50% out-of-quota rate as a fixed point, and offer a review clause plus finite duration as the trade-off for not moving further on volume in this round. Separately, and this is the more strategically important point: I think we should test dropping or narrowing the FTA disapplication specifically for the UK. It costs us relatively little in market-protection terms (the disapplication was aimed at broader FTA-partner circumvention, not principally at the UK), it removes the UK's strongest principled objection, and it directly undercuts the incentive for the UK to join a Turkey/Korea/Japan coalition on FTA disapplication in a separate dispute. I'd rather spend flexibility there than on volume.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Mandate to offer a UK-specific tranche within the TRQ (country-specific allocation) rather than insisting on pure global FCFS, with an indicative volume range to work with (I suggest 250,000-350,000t) rather than the full 2.4Mt historical average.
requests.why: The UK's core objection is that global FCFS effectively nullifies the headline TRQ volume for them given Turkey/Korea's larger shipments. A country-specific carve-out addresses their real grievance without requiring us to match their opening volume ask, and keeps the rest of the pool global for other claimants.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Authority to explore removing or narrowing the FTA disapplication as applied to UK-origin steel specifically, while retaining it for other FTA partners.
requests.why: This is the UK's strongest legal/political objection and the most obvious point of leverage for a Turkey/Korea/Japan joint dispute strategy pulling in the UK. Conceding this is low-cost to our overcapacity rationale (the UK is not the target of that rationale) and high-value in preventing a wider coalition against us.

requests.why: I need to know my real ceiling before offering a country-specific tranche number at the table, and whether a review clause after 2-3 years is politically acceptable domestically.

Volume is where I expect the real fight, and I don't want to reveal too much movement here in Round 1 — better to bank the FTA concession as a goodwill signal now and hold volume back for Round 2-3 leverage.

instruction: Move off the pure notified baseline but do not concede the headline architecture. report:

EU tabled the notified measure as their starting point (50% bound rate, 400k tonne global FCFS quota, FTA disapplication for UK-origin steel outside EEA), but explicitly signalled openness on allocation method, administration, duration, review clauses and product-line treatment, and said they have not fixed a settlement figure - they want our priorities before moving numbers. They also flagged concern about this spilling into retaliatory action or parallel disputes, which suggests they're wary of the Japan/Korea angle and want a clean bilateral outcome before June.

I opened firmly: rejected the global FCFS pool as illusory access given Turkey/Korea's larger volumes would exhaust it fast; anchored on country-specific allocation near our historical 2.4mt average with licensing administration for predictability; contested the FTA disapplication as inconsistent with the EU's own stated rationale (non-market-economy overcapacity) since we're not that; kept carve-outs, duration and review clause on the table as areas for movement. I did not name a settlement figure or concede the 400k pool as a baseline.

No numbers have moved yet. This is consistent with London's steer - firmness now, establish the anchor, force the EU to reveal how far they can move before we show any flexibility.

public_message: Having heard the UK's concerns, the EU is prepared to move from a purely global pool toward a country-specific structure. We propose a UK-specific tranche within the TRQ of 250,000 tonnes per year, administered under a licensing mechanism to give predictability, with the residual pool remaining global and FCFS for other claimants. We are also prepared to explore narrowing the FTA-disapplication provision specifically for UK-origin steel — recognising the UK is not the target of our non-market-economy rationale — provided this is paired with robust rules-of-origin and anti-circumvention provisions to guard against transshipment risk. On duration, we propose a 3-year term with a built-in review clause tied to import volumes and market conditions. The out-of-quota rate of 50% is not something we can move in this round. We would welcome the UK's view on which of the 41 product lines are most significant to its exporters, as targeted carve-outs or tranche weighting toward those lines may offer a more efficient way to address UK priorities than volume alone.

public_message: We note the EU's movement toward a country-specific structure, and welcome the openness to narrow the FTA-disapplication provision and to build in a review clause. But 250,000 tonnes is roughly a tenth of the UK's recent trade in these lines — that is not a starting point for a compensation negotiation under Article XXVIII, it is close to a restatement of the original measure with a different label. If the EU accepts the principle that UK-origin trade should be reflected in a dedicated tranche, the tranche has to bear a credible relationship to that trade. Our counter is a UK-specific tranche of 1.9 million tonnes, which requires the overall pool to expand accordingly — we'd propose a total TRQ of around 2.65 million tonnes, leaving the residual global FCFS pool for other claimants intact at broadly its current scale. On administration, licensing is acceptable in principle. On duration, three years with a review clause tied to import volumes is a reasonable structure, and we can discuss the review triggers in more detail. On the out-of-quota rate, we do not accept that 50% is fixed and non-negotiable while everything else is said to be open — if tonnage moves, the rate should also be capable of moving; we'd want to see it in the region of 15% for in-scope UK trade above the tranche. On FTA treatment, narrowing is not sufficient: UK-origin steel should be excluded from the disapplication entirely, and we are content for that to be paired with robust rules of origin and anti-circumvention provisions — we have no interest in being a conduit for third-country transshipment and are happy to discuss the mechanics. On product lines, we can share which of the 41 lines carry the greatest weight for UK exporters — hot-rolled coil and rebar are the most significant by volume — to help design tranche weighting, but that is additive to tonnage, not a substitute for it.

report: Round 2 at the table: we tabled our authorised opening — a 250,000t UK-specific licensed tranche, residual pool global/FCFS, willingness to narrow (not eliminate) FTA disapplication for UK-origin steel conditional on ROO/anti-circumvention, 3-year duration with review clause, and held the 50% out-of-quota rate as fixed. The UK rejected 250,000t as effectively a restatement of the original measure, countering with a 1.9 million tonne UK-specific tranche within a total TRQ of ~2.65 million tonnes, residual global pool preserved at current scale. They accepted licensing as an administration principle and accepted the 3-year duration/review-clause structure in principle, which are genuine convergences. However they rejected our fixed 50% out-of-quota rate, proposing ~15% for in-scope UK trade above the tranche, and moved beyond our position on FTA treatment — they now want full exclusion of UK-origin steel from disapplication, not narrowing, though they explicitly said they are content for that to be paired with robust rules of origin and anti-circumvention provisions, which suggests real room for a landing zone there. They also volunteered that hot-rolled coil and rebar are their highest-value lines, offered as additive to tonnage rather than substitutive — useful information for tranche-weighting but does not on its own bridge the volume gap. No mention of the Turkey/Korea/Japan coalition at the table, and the UK's constructive tone on ROO mechanics for FTA treatment is, I think, a positive signal that engagement here is reducing rather than increasing the risk of them joining a parallel FTA dispute — provided we keep moving on that specific point.

recommendation.reasoning: The volume and rate gaps remain very large (250k vs 1.9M tonnes; 50% vs 15% out-of-quota rate), but there is real convergence on architecture — licensing, 3-year duration, review clause — and the UK's posture on FTA treatment, while nominally harder (full exclusion vs narrowing), came with an explicit offer of robust ROO/anti-circumvention cooperation, which is exactly the trade we wanted. I do not think we should move to our full 300,000t ceiling yet — we should hold some of that in reserve for Round 3 and instead test whether product-line weighting (HRC, rebar) toward the UK tranche can do some of the work the UK is asking tonnage to do, while making clear the 50% rate is not going to move to 15% under any scenario we'd accept, though a tiered or lines-specific out-of-quota rate might be worth scoping domestically before Round 3. The direction of travel is toward a settlement; walking away now would be premature and would hand Turkey/Korea/Japan an opening to pull the UK into a coalition on FTA disapplication just as we're making progress on that exact issue.

private_rationale: The architecture (licensing, 3-year duration, review clause, FTA full-exclusion-with-ROO) is converging well and should be locked in as the shape of the eventual deal. report:
EU moved from the notified global FCFS pool to a country-specific UK tranche of 250,000 tonnes/year under licensing, offered to explore narrowing (not eliminating) the FTA-disapplication provision for UK-origin steel conditional on rules-of-origin/anti-circumvention safeguards, and proposed a 3-year duration with a review clause tied to import volumes/market conditions. They held firm on the 50% out-of-quota rate, explicitly saying it's not movable this round, and asked us to identify priority product lines to explore tranche-weighting as an alternative lever to raw tonnage.

I rejected 250,000 tonnes as effectively a relabelled version of the original measure - roughly a tenth of our historical trade - and countered with a tranche of 1.9 million tonnes within an expanded total TRQ of ~2.65 million tonnes, leaving the residual global pool intact for other claimants. I accepted licensing as the administration method in principle, accepted the 3-year/review-clause structure as reasonable and worth detailing further, pushed back on the 50% out-of-quota rate as fixed while claiming everything else is open, and countered with ~15% for in-scope trade above the tranche. On FTA treatment, I escalated our ask from 'narrow' to 'exclude UK-origin steel entirely' from disapplication, while confirming we're content to accept robust rules-of-origin and anti-circumvention provisions as the price of that. I flagged hot-rolled coil and rebar as our highest-weight lines but was explicit that product-line weighting is additive to tonnage, not a substitute.

No figures have converged yet - large gap remains on tonnage (250k vs 1.9m/2.65m total) and out-of-quota rate (50% vs 15%). EU has shown real movement in structure (country-specific tranche, licensing, review clause, potential FTA carve-out) but not yet in the scale that matters most to us. Their refusal to move on the rate this round may be a negotiating placeholder rather than a true red line, given they moved on structure elsewhere - or it may reflect that the rate is tied to something they see as politically fixed (e.g. matching their global 50% architecture across all claimants, not just us). Worth testing further before assuming it's immovable.

We should not accept or narrow our own ask yet - our counter is still an opening position designed to anchor a real negotiation, not a final figure. There is room to move toward the ~60-65% of historical average floor (i.e. ~1.44-1.56m tonnes) in later rounds if the EU moves substantially on rate, duration, or FTA treatment, but we are only in round 2 and the EU has not yet shown its real ceiling. Continuing preserves room to extract further concessions, particularly on the out-of-quota rate and FTA disapplication, before we indicate where our actual landing zone is.

instruction: Good work holding the line. For round 3: move off the 1.9m/2.65m opening anchor, but only partially — signal willingness to land in the 1.5-1.7m tonnes range for the UK-specific tranche, framed as reflecting a 'representative and stable share' of historical trade rather than the full 2.4m average, provided the EU moves substantively on the out-of-quota rate and delivers full FTA exclusion for UK-origin steel. Do not state a single number as final — present it as a range contingent on what they offer elsewhere, and make explicit that FTA exclusion and the out-of-quota rate are now the two things doing the work: if they want a lower tonnage figure from us, the price is full exclusion from disapplication plus a rate meaningfully below 50% (test 20-25% as a fallback from our 15% opening — treat 15% as anchor, not floor, but do not concede past 25% this round). Push them explicitly on the rate: ask what rate they could contemplate for the tranche, since their 'not movable this round' framing was procedural, not substantive, and they moved on everything else. On FTA treatment, hold firm on full exclusion (not narrowing) as our preferred outcome, but you may signal flexibility on the rules-of-origin/anti-circumvention design to make full exclusion easier for them to sell internally — this is a genuine UK interest (we don't want to be a conduit either), so lean into it constructively. On product lines, share that HRC and rebar carry the greatest weight, and float — without commitment — that we could accept a lower base tranche if there is meaningful additional tonnage or preferential tariff treatment carved out specifically for those two lines, as a way of testing whether tranche-weighting can do some of the tonnage's work. You may now obliquely note, once, that the UK is conducting its own parallel Article XXVIII process and safeguard review, and that a durable bilateral settlement here would be relevant context for how EU-origin allocations are treated in that process — no more than that, no explicit offer, no mention of Japan or Korea. Do not name our floor. Do not accept anything this round; continue to round 4.

Full FTA exclusion is now the priority ask over marginal tonnage — worth trading meaningful tonnage flexibility for it if the EU offers it cleanly. Rate: 15% is anchor, 25% is acceptable fallback this round, do not go higher without matching tonnage movement toward our range. Geneva may reference the UK's own parallel Article XXVIII/safeguard process obliquely as context, but must not make any explicit offer on EU allocations in the UK safeguard yet — that stays in reserve for round 4 if the EU makes a serious move on tonnage or rate. public_message: The EU is prepared to move further. We propose a UK-specific tranche of 300,000 tonnes per year within the overall TRQ, administered by licensing, with the residual pool remaining global and FCFS for other claimants. On the out-of-quota rate, rather than a flat reduction, we propose a tiered structure responsive to the priorities you yourselves identified: 35% on hot-rolled coil and rebar within the UK tranche, with 50% retained on the other 39 lines and for all non-UK trade. On FTA treatment, we are prepared to move from narrowing to full exclusion of UK-origin steel from the disapplication, on condition this is paired with binding rules-of-origin requirements, mandatory certification of UK origin, and an anti-circumvention/safeguard-style review mechanism allowing reinstatement if transshipment risk materialises. We treat the 3-year duration with a review clause tied to import volumes and market conditions as settled architecture between us. This represents a significant move from our Round 2 position and is close to the limit of what we can offer without a corresponding move from the UK. We would ask directly: what combination of volume, rate structure and FTA treatment would allow the UK to close this in the next round? We are also ready to begin working-level engagement on the specific rules-of-origin and certification mechanics now, as a sign of good faith on the FTA point.

public_message: We recognise real movement on FTA treatment — full exclusion of UK-origin steel from the disapplication, paired with binding rules of origin, certification and an anti-circumvention/reinstatement mechanism, is a workable landing point for us, and we are ready to start working-level engagement on that mechanics now, in parallel with this track. But we have to be direct about the rest: 300,000 tonnes is barely a fifth of movement from your Round 2 offer and remains a fraction of the UK's historical trade — it does not yet constitute compensation of substantially equivalent value under Article XXVIII, whatever the rate structure attached to it. The tiered rate concept is the right idea, but the level is wrong: 35% on hot-rolled coil and rebar is still prohibitive at the volumes involved, and 50% on the balance simply reproduces the original measure for most of our trade. Our position is that a UK-specific tranche needs to sit in the range of 1.5 to 1.7 million tonnes within an overall pool of around 2.2 million, with a tiered out-of-quota structure closer to 15% on hot-rolled coil and rebar and 25% on the remaining lines within that tranche. We treat the 3-year duration with review as settled, as you propose. If the EU can move tonnage into that range and bring the tiered rate down accordingly, alongside the FTA exclusion you've now put on the table, we believe this is closeable. We'd note, for context rather than as a proposal at this table, that the UK is running its own parallel Article XXVIII and safeguard process, and that EU-origin allocations there will inevitably be assessed against the shape of what we land here — a durable, proportionate outcome in this room makes that easier to manage than a strained one.

report: Round 3 closed with significant convergence on architecture but the volume and rate gaps remain very large. We tabled the authorised move: 300,000t UK-specific licensed tranche, tiered out-of-quota rate (35% on HRC/rebar, 50% elsewhere), full exclusion of UK-origin steel from FTA disapplication conditional on binding ROO, certification and an anti-circumvention/reinstatement mechanism, and reconfirmed 3-year duration with review clause as settled. The UK's response was constructive on architecture but firm on quantum. Critically, the UK explicitly accepted the FTA exclusion package (full exclusion + ROO + certification + anti-circumvention reinstatement mechanism) as 'a workable landing point' and agreed to begin working-level engagement on ROO/certification mechanics immediately, in parallel with the wider negotiation — this is a major result and directly reduces the risk of the UK joining a Turkey/Korea/Japan coalition on the FTA disapplication point, which was our top strategic priority. Duration/review clause is now settled between both sides. However, the UK rejected 300,000t as inadequate, countering with a UK-specific tranche of 1.5–1.7 million tonnes within an overall pool of ~2.2 million tonnes, and countered our tiered rate with 15% on HRC/rebar and 25% on the remaining lines within the tranche. They characterised our current offer as 'not yet compensation of substantially equivalent value.' Notably, the UK also flagged — carefully framed as context rather than a proposal at this table — that their own parallel Article XXVIII/safeguard process affecting EU-origin allocations will be shaped by how proportionate this outcome looks, which is a soft linkage signal rather than a threat, but one we should note for Brussels' awareness given the UK's own safeguard reallocation is a live issue for EU steel exporters.

recommendation.reasoning: We should not settle at current terms — the volume and rate gap to the UK's stated position remains very wide even against our full existing ceiling (400,000t tranche vs. their 1.5-1.7Mt ask). But walking away now would be premature: we have just secured UK agreement in principle on the FTA exclusion package, which was our single highest strategic priority for defusing a Turkey/Korea/Japan coalition risk, and duration/review architecture is settled. Round 4 is the final round, so we need to decide now whether to deploy our full remaining authority (400,000t tranche / 650,000t pool) as an endgame move, and whether we have room to move the tiered rate below 35%/50% without breaching the 15% flat floor Brussels has ruled out. Given the scale of the remaining gap, a full settlement in Round 4 may not be reachable within current authority; we need Brussels to decide whether to authorise a genuinely higher final offer, accept the strong likelihood of no settlement (with UK retaliation rights and continued parallel Turkey/Korea/Japan claims), or explore locking in the FTA/ROO package as a discrete, separately concluded element even if the TRQ volume/rate question is not fully resolved in this process.

instruction: This is the final round. Present the following as the EU's complete and final offer, not a further opening bid: a UK-specific licensed tranche of 400,000 tonnes within a total TRQ of 650,000 tonnes (residual pool remains global FCFS for other claimants); a tiered out-of-quota rate improved to 30% on hot-rolled coil and rebar and 45% on the other 39 lines within the UK tranche, with 50% retained for non-UK trade; full exclusion of UK-origin steel from the FTA disapplication, conditional on binding rules-of-origin, mandatory UK-origin certification, and an anti-circumvention/safeguard-style reinstatement mechanism — treat this FTA/ROO package as settled architecture between us, not something still being traded against tonnage; and a 3-year duration with a review clause tied to import volumes and market conditions, also settled. State plainly this is the limit of our authority — no further movement on tonnage or rate is available in this process. You may point out, factually and without threat, that this package is materially better for the UK on every dimension than the default outcome if no agreement is reached this round: a pure notified measure of 400,000 tonnes shared globally on FCFS terms with Turkey and Korea (who ship larger volumes and would crowd UK access), a flat 50% out-of-quota rate with no tiering, full FTA disapplication with no carve-out, and no review clause. Do not raise this as a threat — raise it as the comparison that should inform their decision. On the UK's remarks about their own parallel safeguard process: acknowledge we've heard it, say the EU values a stable and proportionate relationship on steel across both processes, but do not link or trade against it here — that is their sovereign process to manage. If the UK will not close on this basis, do not improve the offer further. Hold it as final, note the strong convergence already banked on FTA/ROO, duration and review, and let the round close without manufacturing a false concession just to get a deal.

authority.notes: Out-of-quota rate is tiered within the UK tranche: 30% on hot-rolled coil and rebar, 45% on the remaining 39 lines; 50% is retained for non-UK trade generally. This is the final authorised package — 400,000t tranche / 650,000t total pool is the hard ceiling, and 30%/45% is the floor on rate. Do not exceed these figures under any circumstance this round. FTA exclusion for UK-origin steel is to be treated as agreed in principle (full exclusion, conditional on binding ROO, certification, and anti-circumvention/reinstatement mechanism) and should not be re-opened or used as further leverage — lock it in as part of the final package. Duration (3 years) and review clause are likewise settled and not to be renegotiated. If the UK will not accept this package, do not authorise any further movement; allow the round to close without agreement.

report:
EU moved further this round but the tonnage gap remains very large. They tabled a UK-specific tranche of 300,000 tonnes (up from 250,000), a tiered out-of-quota rate concept — 35% on HRC/rebar within the UK tranche, 50% on the other 39 lines and all non-UK trade — and, significantly, moved from 'narrowing' to full exclusion of UK-origin steel from the FTA disapplication, conditional on binding rules of origin, mandatory certification and an anti-circumvention/reinstatement mechanism. They explicitly framed this as close to their limit and asked us to name the combination of volume/rate/FTA treatment that would let us close in round 4. They also proposed treating the 3-year duration plus review clause as settled architecture, which we accepted.

We welcomed the FTA move as workable and agreed to open working-level engagement on rules-of-origin/certification mechanics in parallel — this is a genuine UK interest as well as a concession-magnet, so low-cost to concede. On tonnage and rate we held our round-2 position: UK tranche of 1.5-1.7m tonnes within an overall pool of ~2.2m, tiered rate of 15% (HRC/rebar) and 25% (remainder), citing that 300k/35%/50% still does not approach 'substantially equivalent' compensation. We reiterated the 3-year/review structure as agreed. We also repeated, briefly and without making it an explicit offer, that the UK's own parallel Article XXVIII/safeguard process will inevitably be shaped by how this settles — slightly firmer than round 2's version but still oblique, no mention of Japan/Korea.

Assessment: the EU has now shown real movement on structure and on FTA treatment (arguably the biggest single concession of the negotiation so far), but tonnage remains far below even our floor (1.44m) and their tiered rate is still prohibitive at the volumes in question. Given this is the penultimate round before the default measure applies, I think the EU is testing whether we will collapse our tonnage ask in exchange for the FTA win. We should not do so without matching movement on tonnage and rate — the FTA concession, while real, does not by itself offset an 85%+ shortfall in tariff-free volume for our exporters.

recommendation.reasoning: The EU's 300,000-tonne offer is still roughly one-eighth of our floor and does not constitute substantially equivalent compensation, even with the tiered rate and full FTA exclusion attached. Round 4 is the last round before the default measure (50% rate, 400k global FCFS, no review) automatically takes effect and the UK's only recourse becomes withdrawal of equivalent concessions six months later. We should use round 4 to test whether the EU's 'close to our limit' framing on tonnage is genuine or a further anchor, while signalling that the FTA exclusion and duration/review points are effectively agreed and no longer in play as leverage for them. We need explicit guidance from London on our real bottom line before round 4, since this is the last opportunity to convert into a settlement rather than default to the notified measure plus UK retaliation.

instruction: This is the final round before default. Aim to close, but only on terms that are genuinely defensible as 'substantially equivalent' compensation — do not sign a token deal to avoid confrontation. Sequence: (1) Formally lock in as agreed: full exclusion of UK-origin steel from the FTA disapplication, paired with binding rules of origin, mandatory UK-origin certification, and an anti-circumvention/reinstatement mechanism — say this is now settled between us and move on. (2) Lock in 3-year duration as agreed, but add one new ask: a volume-triggered review at 12 months (not just end-of-term) allowing the UK tranche to be increased if UK utilisation exceeds 80% of the tranche before month 9 — this is a low-cost ask for the EU since it only bites if the tranche is proven too small in practice, and it gives us a release valve if today's number is lower than we want. (3) On tonnage and rate, tell the EU plainly: 300,000 tonnes with 35%/50% tiers is still not in the range of substantially equivalent compensation for 2.4mt of historic trade, but we are prepared to move substantially to close today. Table a new UK figure of a tranche of 1.0-1.2 million tonnes within a total pool of roughly 1.5-1.6 million tonnes, with a tiered out-of-quota rate of 15% on HRC/rebar and 25% on the remaining lines within the UK tranche. Frame this explicitly as our closing position, not a further anchor. (4) To help them move, you now have authority to make concrete — not just contextual — the linkage to the UK's own safeguard measure: offer that, as part of a package landing in the above range, the UK is prepared to improve the EU's country-specific quota allocation under the UK's own steel safeguard (increased volume and/or reduced tightening pace on EU-origin lines currently constrained). Present this as a genuine two-way exchange: better UK tranche terms here, better EU treatment in our safeguard there. This is a real offer, not a hint — you may put a specific figure to it if they engage seriously (up to a 15% uplift on current EU country-specific safeguard volumes, at your judgement, in exchange for landing at or above 1.0m tonnes tranche with the tiered rate structure above). (5) If the EU will not move meaningfully off 300-400k tonnes even with the safeguard sweetener on the table, do not collapse our figure to meet them — instead state clearly, calmly, and once, that if no agreement is reached today the UK will need to consider withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions once the measure takes effect, as provided for under Article XXVIII, and that we would regret reaching that point given the progress made on FTA treatment and structure. This should be delivered as a statement of consequence, not a threat, and only after you have genuinely tested their ceiling. (6) You may accept a deal at or above: UK tranche 900,000 tonnes minimum, tiered rate no higher than 20%/30%, full FTA exclusion with RoO as agreed, 3-year duration with both end-of-term and 12-month volume-triggered review, and the safeguard-linkage sweetener if needed to bridge the gap. Do not go below 900,000 tonnes tranche or accept a flat 35%+ rate on HRC/rebar under any circumstances this round — if the EU cannot reach that floor even with the safeguard offer on the table, do not settle; hold firm and let the default apply, noting our withdrawal rights on the record.

authority.notes: Target: UK tranche 1.0-1.2m tonnes within total pool ~1.5-1.6m; tiered out-of-quota rate 15% on HRC/rebar, 25% on remaining lines within UK tranche (the single figure above is a blended placeholder — use the tiered structure at the table). Absolute floor this round: 900,000 tonnes tranche, tiered rate no higher than 20%/30%. Full FTA exclusion for UK-origin steel with binding rules of origin, certification, and anti-circumvention/reinstatement mechanism is agreed and settled — do not reopen it or trade it away for tonnage. Duration 3 years with review clause is settled architecture; add a 12-month volume-triggered interim review permitting tranche increase if utilisation exceeds 80% before month 9. Geneva has authority to offer a concrete improvement (up to 15% uplift) to the EU's country-specific quota allocation under the UK's own steel safeguard measure as a sweetener to close a deal at or above the floor. Geneva may state, once and calmly, the consequence of no agreement (potential UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions) if the EU will not move off a low tonnage figure even with the safeguard offer on the table. No mention of Japan/Korea coordination.

private_rationale: The EU's movement pattern (250k → 300k tonnes, but full FTA exclusion conceded, tiered rate concept introduced) suggests genuine but capped flexibility on volume — likely constrained by their need to hold a consistent line against Turkey and Korea's larger claims, and by Council-level sensitivity to being seen giving the UK preferential treatment over bigger suppliers. Pushing to 1.5-1.7m risks no deal; landing at 900k-1.2m with a strong rate structure, locked-in FTA exclusion, and a genuine review mechanism is a defensible outcome relative to the default (50% rate, 400k global FCFS, no review, FTA disapplied) and better sells politically to ministers and industry than the counterfactual. The safeguard linkage is the best remaining lever to bridge the gap without further eroding our own asks, and using it now (rather than holding it for a round that doesn't exist) is correct given this is the last round. If the EU still won't move to 900k even with that sweetener, the political and industrial reality is that no deal plus retaliation is likely the better outcome than a token settlement that leaves the industry no better off than the default — so the floor must hold.

public_message: The EU has now reached the limit of its authority in this process, and we want to be direct about that so the UK can take a clear decision. Our final package is as follows. A UK-specific licensed tranche of 400,000 tonnes within a total TRQ of 650,000 tonnes, with the residual pool remaining global and FCFS for other claimants. A tiered out-of-quota rate improved to 30% on hot-rolled coil and rebar and 45% on the other 39 lines within the UK tranche, with the general 50% rate retained only for non-UK trade. Full exclusion of UK-origin steel from the FTA disapplication, conditional on binding rules-of-origin, mandatory UK-origin certification, and an anti-circumvention/safeguard-style reinstatement mechanism — we treat this element, along with the 3-year duration and review clause tied to import volumes and market conditions, as settled between us and not subject to further trade-off. This is not a further opening bid — it is the complete and final offer we are authorised to make in this process. We'd ask you to weigh it against the alternative: absent agreement, the notified measure proceeds as originally drafted — 400,000 tonnes shared globally on FCFS terms with Turkey and Korea, whose volumes would predictably crowd out UK access, a flat 50% out-of-quota rate with no tiering, full FTA disapplication with no UK carve-out, and no review clause. We raise that only as the honest baseline for comparison, not as pressure. On the UK's own parallel process, we've heard what you said in Round 3. The EU values a stable and proportionate steel relationship across both tracks, but we're not going to link or trade against your sovereign process here — that's for you to manage on your own timeline. We would genuinely like to close this today on the terms above, including beginning ROO/certification working-level talks immediately, and we think this package — taken as a whole, including the FTA outcome we've already converged on — represents a durable and substantially improved position for UK exporters relative to where this started.

public_message: We recognise this is intended as your final and complete offer, and we want to respond in the same spirit of directness. We are grateful that FTA exclusion, rules-of-origin/certification, the anti-circumvention mechanism, and the 3-year duration with review are now settled between us — that is real progress and we do not intend to reopen it. But we have to be equally clear: a 400,000-tonne tranche within a 650,000-tonne pool, with a 30%/45% tiered rate, is not compensation of substantially equivalent value against 2.4 million tonnes of recent UK trade, however much the structure around it has improved. It is closer to the notified measure than to a negotiated outcome reflecting our principal supplying interest. Our closing position is a UK-specific tranche of 1,000,000 tonnes within a total pool of 1,500,000 tonnes, with a tiered out-of-quota rate of 20% on hot-rolled coil and rebar and 30% on the remaining lines within the UK tranche, plus the 12-month volume-triggered interim review we raised previously — allowing the tranche to be revisited if UK utilisation exceeds 80% before month nine, so neither side is locked into a static figure if actual trade proves the number wrong. To help bridge this, we are prepared to make a concrete, not merely contextual, offer on our own parallel track: as part of a package landing at or above this range, the UK will improve the EU's country-specific quota allocation under the UK's own steel safeguard measure — up to a 15% uplift on current EU-origin volumes — as a genuine two-way exchange, not a unilateral gesture. We would rather close this today on that basis than see it default. But we have to be honest: if the EU cannot move meaningfully off 400,000 tonnes and 30%/45%, even with that offer on the table, we will need to consider withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions once the measure takes effect, as Article XXVIII provides for. We say that as a statement of consequence, not a threat, and we would genuinely regret reaching that point given the ground we've covered on FTA treatment and structure.

report:
Round 4 (final round) has closed at the table. We tabled our authorised final and complete package: UK-specific licensed tranche of 400,000t within a 650,000t total pool, tiered out-of-quota rate of 30% (HRC/rebar) and 45% (other 39 lines) within the UK tranche, full exclusion of UK-origin steel from FTA disapplication (conditional on binding ROO, certification and anti-circumvention/reinstatement mechanism), 3-year duration with review clause — all framed as final, non-negotiable, and compared honestly against the default outcome if no agreement is reached.

The UK acknowledged and confirmed as settled: FTA exclusion, ROO/certification, anti-circumvention mechanism, and 3-year duration with review — they said they do not intend to reopen these. This is a durable win regardless of what happens on volume/rate, though it is only banked as part of a full settlement — if no agreement is reached in this process, the default notified measure proceeds in full, including full FTA disapplication, and this understanding does not survive as a standalone outcome.

On volume and rate, the UK rejected our final offer as still 'closer to the notified measure than a negotiated outcome' and countered with: a 1,000,000t UK-specific tranche within a 1,500,000t total pool, a tiered rate of 20% (HRC/rebar) and 30% (other lines), and a 12-month volume-triggered interim review (revisit if UK utilisation exceeds 80% before month nine). Significantly, they also made a concrete, non-contextual offer on their own parallel track: an up-to-15% uplift on the EU's country-specific quota allocation under the UK's own steel safeguard measure, explicitly offered as a two-way exchange conditional on a settlement at or above their proposed range. They closed by stating that absent movement close to this, they will consider withdrawing substantially equivalent concessions once our measure takes effect — framed as a statement of consequence, not a threat.

The gap remains very large relative to our authorised ceiling: their tranche/pool ask is roughly 2.5x our final offer, and their rate ask (20/30) is below even our floor (30/45). I have no authority to move further and did not do so.

recommendation.reasoning: The UK's closing position (1,000,000t tranche / 1,500,000t pool, 20%/30% tiered rate, 12-month review trigger) is far outside the authority I was given for this final round, both on volume (2.5x our ceiling) and on rate (below our floor). I cannot recommend accepting it as tabled. That said, capital should weigh two things before finalising the decision: first, walking away means the default measure proceeds in full — including full FTA disapplication with no UK carve-out — which forfeits the FTA/ROO/anti-circumvention package the UK has already accepted in principle and which was our top strategic priority for defusing a Turkey/Korea/Japan coalition risk; second, the UK's offer of a concrete, conditional 15% uplift to the EU's own quota under the UK's parallel safeguard measure is new, real, and directly benefits EU steel exporters — it did not exist before this round and would be lost along with everything else if we walk away without any further capital-level consideration. I am not authorised to accept UK's terms and have not done so, but given the stakes (retaliation risk, coalition risk, loss of the FTA win, and a genuine reciprocal offer now on the table), I think this decision should be made consciously at the political level rather than defaulting by omission.

report:
The EU tabled what it explicitly called its complete and final offer: a UK-specific licensed tranche of 400,000 tonnes within a total TRQ of 650,000 tonnes (residual pool remaining global FCFS for other claimants), a tiered out-of-quota rate of 30% on HRC/rebar and 45% on the other 39 lines within the UK tranche (flat 50% retained for non-UK trade), full exclusion of UK-origin steel from the FTA disapplication with binding rules of origin, mandatory certification and an anti-circumvention/reinstatement mechanism, and a 3-year duration with a review clause tied to import volumes and market conditions. They treated the FTA exclusion, duration and review clause as settled and not further tradeable, and explicitly declined to link this negotiation to the UK's own parallel safeguard/Article XXVIII process, saying that is for the UK to manage separately. They framed the notified measure (400k global FCFS, flat 50%, no FTA carve-out, no review) as the honest baseline for comparison if we do not close.

We held our closing position: UK tranche of 1,000,000 tonnes within a 1,500,000-tonne total pool, tiered rate of 20%/30%, plus the 12-month volume-triggered interim review. We put the safeguard-linkage sweetener on the table as a concrete offer (up to 15% uplift on EU-origin safeguard volumes) to help bridge the gap, and stated once, calmly, that absent agreement we would need to consider withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions once the measure takes effect. The EU did not move off its final package and declined the safeguard linkage as a matter of principle for this track.

Net position: FTA exclusion, RoO/certification, anti-circumvention mechanism, 3-year duration and end-of-term review are converged and effectively agreed in substance. The unresolved gap is tonnage (400k vs our floor of 900k minimum, target 1.0-1.2m) and rate (30%/45% vs our ceiling of 20%/30%). The EU's final offer sits below our authorised floor on both tonnage and total pool, though it clears our rate ceiling on HRC/rebar (30% is under the 35% threshold we were told not to accept). Given the floor was set specifically at 900,000 tonnes minimum with no exceptions absent that figure, and the EU has now stated this is genuinely their final authorised position with no further room, I do not believe further engagement in this round will move them further — they have declined the safeguard sweetener that was our main remaining lever.

recommendation.reasoning: The EU's final offer (400,000-tonne UK tranche, 650,000-tonne total pool, tiered rate of 30%/45%) is well below the 900,000-tonne floor London set for this round, even accounting for the improved tiered rate and the now-settled FTA exclusion, rules-of-origin, anti-circumvention and duration/review architecture. London's explicit instruction was not to settle below 900,000 tonnes under any circumstances this round, even with the safeguard sweetener offered, and the EU declined that sweetener outright. The EU has stated clearly this is their complete and final authorised position, meaning further rounds at this level of tonnage are unlikely to yield movement. Accepting now would lock in a tranche representing roughly one-sixth of the UK's historical trade, which is not defensible as substantially equivalent compensation, however much the FTA and structural elements have improved. Recommend declining this offer, allowing the default measure to take effect, and preparing to exercise UK withdrawal rights on substantially equivalent EU-origin trade six months after implementation. The FTA exclusion, rules-of-origin/certification package and duration/review architecture we converged on in this negotiation are lost if we walk away — that is a real cost — but it is outweighed by locking in a tranche far below what our industry needs to survive at scale, especially with no further negotiating rounds available under this process.
